content: Antileukoproteinase, also referred to as secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor (SLPI), is an enzyme encoded by the SLPI gene in humans. It is a highly cationic, single-chain protein that contains eight intramolecular disulfide bonds. SLPI is abundantly present in bronchial, cervical, and nasal mucosa, as well as in saliva and seminal fluids. This protein functions as an inhibitor of several proteases, including human leukocyte elastase, cathepsin G, trypsin, neutrophil elastase, and mast cell chymase. Structural studies using X-ray crystallography have revealed that SLPI consists of two homologous domains, one containing 53 amino acids and the other 54 amino acids. The C-terminal domain is responsible for its anti-protease activity, while the N-terminal domain does not have a clearly defined function. The SLPI gene encodes a secreted protein that serves as an inhibitor to protect epithelial tissues from damage caused by serine proteases. It is found in various bodily secretions, such as seminal plasma, cervical mucus, and bronchial secretions. SLPI has a high affinity for proteases like trypsin, leukocyte elastase, and cathepsin G. By inhibiting these proteases, SLPI plays a critical role in the immune response, safeguarding epithelial surfaces from damage caused by endogenous proteolytic enzymes. Additionally, SLPI is believed to possess broad-spectrum antibiotic properties. The SLPI gene is expressed in cells located at numerous mucosal surfaces, including tissues in the lungs, cervix, seminal vesicles, and parotid ducts. It is one of the most abundant proteins in nasal epithelial lining fluid and other nasal secretions. The expression of SLPI in tissues is compartmentalized, with the highest levels observed in the endocervix and the lowest levels in the endometrium of postmenopausal women. Hormonal treatments have been shown to modulate SLPI expression differently along the reproductive tract. Several diseases, such as emphysema, cystic fibrosis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, are associated with elevated levels of neutrophil elastase, an enzyme that can cause significant tissue damage. SLPI serves as a major defense mechanism against the destructive effects of neutrophil elastase on pulmonary and epithelial tissues. In secretions, SLPI is the predominant elastase inhibitor, while α1-antitrypsin is the primary elastase inhibitor in tissues. In certain diseases, the protective effects of SLPI and α1-antitrypsin are overwhelmed by excessive neutrophil elastase activity, leading to tissue damage. Recombinant human SLPI has been proposed as a potential therapeutic agent for managing symptoms of cystic fibrosis, genetic emphysema, and asthma. SLPI levels have been monitored in various pathological conditions. Elevated SLPI levels in nasal secretions and bronchoalveolar fluids may indicate inflammatory lung conditions or allergic reactions, while increased SLPI levels in plasma may suggest pneumonia. Higher SLPI levels in saliva and plasma have also been associated with HIV infection, which is consistent with the rarity of HIV transmission through oral-to-oral contact. SLPI exhibits antiviral activity by interfering with protease-mediated processes, such as viral entry into host cells and replication of viral genetic material. Studies have demonstrated that reduced SLPI levels in saliva correspond to diminished anti-HIV activity. Notably, SLPI’s anti-HIV properties are observed under physiological conditions, making it a subject of significant interest. Furthermore, an inverse correlation has been identified between SLPI levels and high-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection, suggesting that elevated SLPI levels provide protection against HPV infection. SLPI has been shown to interact with specific proteins on the plasma membrane of T-cells, such as PLSCR1 and PLSCR4, particularly near the CD4 receptor. This interaction is hypothesized to contribute to SLPI’s ability to inhibit HIV infection. Additionally, SLPI can bind to the Annexin A2/S100A10 heterotetramer (A2t), a co-factor for HIV infection, on the surface of macrophages. This interaction with A2t has also been demonstrated to block the uptake and infection of epithelial cells by HPV.
